title: Transitivity, Transitive Closure and Warshall
quickIdea: Transitivity is a closure condition on chains of length two. The transitive closure adds exactly the pairs forced by longer and longer chains, and it is what Warshall computes.
remember: R is transitive when (a, b) in R and (b, c) in R implies (a, c) in R, for all a, b, c.
Equivalently R is transitive exactly when the composite R composed with R is a subset of R.
Transitivity is not implied by reflexivity or symmetry, and it does not imply either: the empty relation is transitive but not reflexive.
The transitive closure of R is the smallest transitive relation containing R; it equals the union of R, R squared, R cubed, ... over all positive lengths.
The reflexive-transitive closure adds the diagonal pairs to the transitive closure, and it is what reachability in a directed graph means.
Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure in time cubic in the number of elements, by repeatedly allowing one more intermediate vertex.

A relation can be symmetric and transitive without being reflexive: the empty relation on a non-empty set is the simplest example, and on {1, 2, 3} the relation {(1,1), (2,2), (1,2), (2,1)} is symmetric and transitive while (3,3) is missing.
Transitivity is the property that fails when a question writes 'or' where it should write 'and': a disjunctive condition on two coordinates usually loses transitivity.
Checking transitivity by hand means looking for a chain whose shortcut is missing; one missing shortcut is enough to refute it.

example.prompt: A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1,2), (2,3)}. Is R transitive? Give its transitive closure.
example.work: The chain (1,2) then (2,3) forces (1,3), which is not in R, so R is not transitive. R squared contains (1,3) and nothing else new, and R cubed is empty, so the process stops.
example.answer: R is not transitive; its transitive closure is {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3)}.

gateAngle: GATE CS 2016 Set 2 Q.26 defines R on pairs of naturals by a <= c or b <= d and asks about reflexivity and transitivity: reflexivity holds, transitivity fails, and a single chain refutes it.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: See GATE CS 2016 Set 2 Q.26 in the linked PYQs.
variations.answer: Option (B): P is true and Q is false.
variations.why: a <= a is always true, so every pair is related to itself. For transitivity, (2,10) R (3,1) holds because 2 <= 3 and (3,1) R (1,2) holds because 1 <= 2, but (2,10) R (1,2) fails because 2 <= 1 is false and 10 <= 2 is false.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4} let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4)}. How many pairs does the transitive closure add?
variations.why: Chains of length two give (1,3) and (2,4); the chain of length three 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 gives (1,4). Chains of length four do not exist, so the closure has six pairs in all.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is a symmetric and transitive relation necessarily reflexive?
variations.why: Reflexivity needs a diagonal pair for every element. With A = {1, 2, 3} the relation {(1,2), (2,1), (1,1), (2,2)} is symmetric and transitive, yet (3,3) is missing, so it is not reflexive.

trap.what: Checking transitivity only on the pairs you happened to write down, or assuming that a symmetric transitive relation must be reflexive.
trap.why: Transitivity quantifies over every chain, including chains built from pairs you did not list; and reflexivity is an independent condition that symmetry plus transitivity does not supply.
trap.counterexample: A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1,1), (2,2), (1,2), (2,1)}. It is symmetric and transitive, yet (3,3) is not in R, so it is not reflexive. Note that {(1,2), (2,1)} alone is not even transitive: it forces (1,1).

check.question: R = {(1,1), (1,2), (2,2)} on {1, 2}. Is R transitive? Is it symmetric?
check.explanation: The only chain is (1,1) then (1,2), which forces (1,2) - present. Symmetry fails because (1,2) is in R while (2,1) is not.
